pos: n. (the County Galway monastic site of Colman mac Duagh, with the leaning round tower)
etymology: Irish Cill Mhic Duach, the church of the son of Duach, from its seventh-century founder.
biblical_def: Kilmacduagh in County Galway, below the Burren, was founded in the early seventh century by Colman mac Duagh, and became the head of a diocese that survived until it was united with Galway. The site holds a cathedral, several smaller churches, and a round tower about a hundred feet high, the tallest in Ireland and visibly out of plumb, leaning some two feet from the vertical. The lean has been there since at least the eighteenth century and the tower has not fallen. The dictionary records Kilmacduagh for that tower, which supplies the better part of a sermon on its own. A structure can be out of true and still stand for a thousand years, and that is exactly the danger: nothing in the building announces the fault, and the people beneath it grow used to the angle. So with doctrine. The Psalmist asks the question that matters, “If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?” (Psa 11:3), and the apostolic instrument for detecting a lean is not the eye but the plumb line of a text: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21), with “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16) naming what the line is made of.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a plumb line as a line perpendicular to the horizon; perpendicular as exactly upright; a foundation as the basis of an edifice; to prove as to try by a standard; and inspiration as the infusion of ideas by the Spirit.
webster_full: PLUMB-LINE, n. A line perpendicular to the plane of the horizon; a line directed to the center of the earth.
PERPENDICULAR, a. Falling directly on another line at right angles; exactly upright.
FOUNDATION, n. The basis of an edifice; that part of an edifice which lies on the ground.
PROVE, v.t. To try; to ascertain some unknown quality or truth by an experiment, or by a test or standard.
INSPIRATION, n. The infusion of ideas into the mind by the Holy Spirit.
scriptures: Psa 11:3
If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?
Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
Psa 19:7
The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple.
corruption_summary: Seventh-century foundation of Colman mac Duagh in County Galway, with the tallest and most conspicuously leaning round tower in Ireland.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a thing out of true can stand a long time. Kilmacduagh's tower has leaned for centuries without falling, and the Psalmist's question remains the right one, “If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?” (Psa 11:3), because the danger of a slow lean is that nobody notices the angle.

The live temptation is to take survival as proof of soundness — it has lasted, therefore it is upright. Scripture gives a test instead of a presumption, “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21), and names the straight edge it is applied with, “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16). The Psalmist calls that edge perfect and says what it does: “The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul” (Psa 19:7).

pos: n. (the County Cork Franciscan friary founded about 1240, among the earliest in Ireland)
etymology: Irish Tigh Molaga, the house of Molaga, a seventh-century saint; the friary is far later than the name.
biblical_def: Timoleague on the Argideen estuary in west Cork takes its name from a seventh-century church of Molaga, but the great ruin on the shore is a Franciscan friary, founded about 1240 and so among the first Franciscan houses in Ireland. It was enlarged repeatedly, served a wide district, and traded through the estuary; the friars were noted locally for importing wine. It was burned by English forces in 1642 and never recovered, though friars are recorded attached to the place long afterwards. The dictionary records Timoleague for the Franciscan arrival, because the friars are the medieval church's most genuine attempt to answer a real problem. Monks stayed behind walls and the people were untaught; the friars went out, preached in the open, and lived on alms. The impulse matches the commission, “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations” (Mat 28:19), and the method matches the charge, “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2). What the dictionary cannot grant is the vow of poverty as merit, since “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9) excludes it as firmly as it excludes a rich abbey's endowment.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a friar as a brother of a religious order; a mendicant as a beggar, one of a begging order; alms as what is given to the poor; to itinerate as to travel from place to place; and poverty as destitution of property.
webster_full: FRIAR, n. An appellation common to the monks of all orders; a brother of a religious order.
MENDICANT, n. A beggar; one of the begging fraternity of the Romish church.
ALMS, n. Any thing given gratuitously to relieve the poor, as money, food, or clothing.
ITINERATE, v.i. To travel from place to place, particularly for the purpose of preaching.
POVERTY, n. Destitution of property; indigence; want of convenient means of subsistence.
scriptures: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
Eph 2:9
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe.
corruption_summary: One of Ireland's earliest Franciscan friaries, founded about 1240 on the Argideen estuary, burned in 1642.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the friars diagnosed the right disease. People were untaught, and the remedy is to go to them: “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations” (Mat 28:19), and then “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2). Open-air preaching to Cork farmers is closer to the apostolic pattern than a choir office behind a wall, and the dictionary says so.

The live temptation is to let the good diagnosis carry the bad prescription. Voluntary poverty was presented as meritorious, and Paul shuts that door for rich and poor alike: “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9). What God has actually appointed is not a lifestyle but a message, “it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe” (1Co 1:21).

pos: n. (the island monastery of Molaise in Lower Lough Erne, with the finest round tower in Ireland)
etymology: Irish Daimhinis, the ox island; anglicised through Devenish.
biblical_def: Devenish is an island in Lower Lough Erne in County Fermanagh, where Molaise founded a monastery in the sixth century. It was raided by Vikings in 837 and burned in 1157, and rebuilt each time; an Augustinian priory of St Mary was established there in the twelfth century and the site remained in use until the seventeenth. Devenish keeps a round tower of about 1160 that is reckoned the most perfect in Ireland, built of finely jointed stone with a carved cornice of four heads beneath the cap — the only decorated round-tower cornice known. The dictionary records Devenish for the quality of that stonework, and for the fact that it was raised on an island that had already been burned twice. Men who knew the raiders would come back built carefully anyway. That is a species of faith, and Scripture names it without flattery: “your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1Co 15:58) is the promise, and “let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” (Gal 6:9) is the exhortation to people whose work may well be destroyed again.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a cornice as the uppermost member of a column's entablature; masonry as the art of building with stone; to raze as to demolish; perseverance as persistence in a design; and labour as toil.
webster_full: CORNICE, n. In architecture, the uppermost member of the entablature of a column, or the highest projection.
MASONRY, n. The art or occupation of a mason; the work or performance of a mason.
RAZE, v.t. To subvert; to overthrow; to destroy; to level with the ground.
PERSEVERANCE, n. Persistence in any thing undertaken; continued pursuit or prosecution of any business or enterprise begun.
LABOUR, n. Exertion of muscular strength, or bodily exertion which occasions weariness; toil; work.
scriptures: Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
Gal 6:9
And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it.
Ecc 4:9
Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.
corruption_summary: Sixth-century island monastery of Molaise in Lough Erne, twice burned, with the finest and only carved round-tower cornice in Ireland.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is working well at something that may not last. Devenish had been burned before its best tower was built, and Paul's promise is attached to the labour itself: “your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1Co 15:58). The exhortation assumes discouragement and answers it, “let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” (Gal 6:9).

The live temptation is to read durability as divine approval, so that what survives was blessed and what burned was not. The Psalmist prays rather than presumes, “establish thou the work of our hands upon us” (Psa 90:17), and the ordinary wisdom that built the thing is Solomon's, “Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.” (Ecc 4:9) — men working together for a reward they may not see.

pos: n. (the Strangford Lough monastery of Mochaoi, site of the oldest excavated tide mill in the world)
etymology: Irish Naendruim, the nine ridges; the site is on Mahee Island, named from Mochaoi.
biblical_def: Nendrum on Mahee Island in Strangford Lough was founded, tradition says, by Mochaoi in the fifth century, and it was excavated in the 1920s, revealing a monastery laid out in three concentric dry-stone enclosures with the church, round tower stump, and a school at the centre. Excavation of the shoreline in the 1990s produced something more remarkable still: the remains of a tide mill with timbers felled in 619 and a second phase dated to 787 — the earliest excavated tide mill anywhere in the world. Monks had dammed a pool, let the tide fill it, and ground their grain on the ebb. The dictionary records Nendrum for that mill, because it is the best available evidence that the early Irish monasteries were places of applied intelligence and not merely of copying. Scripture makes such work honourable without making it holy: “establish thou the work of our hands upon us” (Psa 90:17) is the prayer over the work of our hands, and “your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1Co 15:58) is the promise, neither requiring a tonsure.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a mill as an engine for grinding; a tide as the alternate rise and fall of the sea; an enclosure as ground surrounded by a fence; ingenuity as skill in invention; and handiwork as work done by hand.
webster_full: MILL, n. A complicated engine or machine for grinding and reducing to fine particles, grain, fruit or other substance.
TIDE, n. The alternate rising and falling of the sea, which happens twice in a little more than twenty-four hours.
ENCLOSURE, n. The act of enclosing; the separation of land from common ground by a fence; a space enclosed.
INGENUITY, n. The quality or power of ready invention; skill or acuteness in contrivance.
HANDIWORK, n. Work done by the hands; hence, work of any kind.
scriptures: And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it.
Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
Gal 6:9
And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
corruption_summary: Early monastery on Strangford Lough, excavated to reveal three concentric enclosures and the world's oldest known tide mill, of 619 and 787.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honour of competent work. Monks at Nendrum harnessed the tide eleven centuries before the phrase renewable energy existed, and the Psalmist's prayer covers it exactly: “establish thou the work of our hands upon us” (Psa 90:17). Paul's promise is attached to such labour, “your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1Co 15:58).

The live temptation is to treat the achievement as evidence for the monastic vocation itself. It is evidence for applied intelligence, which God gives widely. The exhortation “let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” (Gal 6:9) is addressed to every working Christian, and the only arrangement Scripture requires of a community is the modest “Let all things be done decently and in order.” (1Co 14:40).

pos: n. (the Burgundian abbey founded 910, head of the first great monastic reform and of an order of hundreds of houses)
etymology: From the Latin estate name Cluniacum; the order's adjective is Cluniac.
biblical_def: Cluny in Burgundy was founded in 910 by William the Pious, duke of Aquitaine, who did something unusual in the foundation charter: he renounced all rights over the house for himself and his heirs and placed it directly under the apostolic see, which freed it from the lay and episcopal interference that had corrupted most tenth-century monasteries. Under a succession of long-lived and able abbots — Odo, Majolus, Odilo, Hugh and Peter the Venerable — Cluny became the head of a centralised order of hundreds of dependent priories across Europe, and the engine of the reform that preceded and fed the papal reform of the eleventh century. Cluny III, begun in 1088, was the largest church in Christendom until the new St Peter's, and it was destroyed after the French Revolution. The dictionary records Cluny for what success did to it. The reform was real, and within two centuries the house was wealthy, its liturgy had swelled until the offices filled the day, and it needed reforming in turn. “Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works” (Rev 2:5) is the pattern Christ prescribes, and “Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body” (Col 2:23) names the drift exactly.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a liturgy as a form of prayers; an office as a form of worship or devotion; exemption as freedom from a duty; reform as a change from worse to better; and will-worship is given under worship as superstitious devotion of man's own devising.
webster_full: LITURGY, n. A form of prayers; the established formulas for public worship, or the entire ritual for public worship.
OFFICE, n. A formulary of devotion; the daily service of the breviary, as the office of the Virgin.
EXEMPTION, n. The act of exempting; the state of being free or excused from a charge or duty.
REFORM, v.t. To change from worse to better; to amend; to correct; to restore to a former good state.
WORSHIP, n. Chiefly and eminently, the act of paying divine honors to the Supreme Being.
scriptures: Rev 2:5
Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place, except thou repent.
Col 2:23
Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh.
Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her.
corruption_summary: Burgundian abbey founded 910 with immunity from lay control, head of the first great monastic reform and of a centralised order of hundreds of priories.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that reforms institutionalise and then need reforming. Cluny began by renouncing a patron's rights and ended as the richest corporation in Burgundy. Christ's prescription is a return and not a restructuring: “Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works” (Rev 2:5).

The live temptation is to credit the elaboration of the liturgy as devotion's growth. Paul has a term for worship a man designs for himself, “Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body” (Col 2:23), and warns against the whole machinery of inherited human practice, “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men” (Col 2:8). The corrective is the shortest sentence in the Gospels on the subject: “But one thing is needful” (Luk 10:42).

pos: n. (the Burgundian abbey founded 1098, mother house of the Cistercian order and of the Charter of Charity)
etymology: French Citeaux from Latin Cistercium, probably from cisterna, a reedy marsh; the order's name follows the Latin.
biblical_def: Citeaux was founded in 1098 when Robert of Molesme left his own abbey with some twenty monks to keep the Rule of Benedict as written, without the accumulated additions of Cluniac practice. Under its third abbot, the Englishman Stephen Harding, the new house produced the Carta Caritatis, the Charter of Charity, a constitution of remarkable sobriety: each abbey autonomous, visited annually by the abbot of its mother house, with a general chapter of all abbots meeting yearly at Citeaux. The Cistercians rejected elaborate building, coloured glass, and manorial rents, farmed their own land through granges, and spread to more than five hundred houses within a century. The dictionary records Citeaux for the Charter and the principle behind it: go back to the text and strip off what has grown on it. That instinct is the Reformation's, four centuries early, and it is right in method. “Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein” (Jer 6:16) commands precisely that enquiry, and “Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works” (Rev 2:5) is its New Testament form. What Citeaux could not do was apply the method to the Rule itself.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a charter as a written instrument of grant; a chapter as an assembly of monks; austerity as severity of manners; a grange as a monastery farm; and simplicity as freedom from artifice.
webster_full: CHARTER, n. A written instrument, executed with usual forms, given as evidence of a grant, contract, or whatever is done between man and man.
CHAPTER, n. An assembly of the monks of a convent, or of a religious order; a corporation of clergymen.
AUSTERITY, n. Severity of manners or life; rigor; strictness; harsh discipline.
GRANGE, n. A farm, with the buildings; in England, a farm belonging to a monastery.
SIMPLICITY, n. Plainness; freedom from artificial ornament; artlessness of mind.
scriptures: Jer 6:16
Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.
Rev 2:5
Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place, except thou repent.
Therefore, brethren, stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle.
Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
corruption_summary: Burgundian abbey of 1098, mother house of the Cistercians, whose Charter of Charity gave the order its sober constitution.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the method. Citeaux went back to a written rule and scraped off the accretions, and Jeremiah commands that enquiry in so many words: “Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein” (Jer 6:16). Christ's own reforming word is of the same shape, “Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works” (Rev 2:5).

The live temptation is to think the method self-validating, so that any return to an older document counts as reform. It does not; what is returned to must be the right document. Paul's traditions are apostolic and written, “stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle” (2Th 2:15), and the testing never stops, “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21). Citeaux applied the knife to Cluny and never to Benedict.

pos: n. (the Cistercian abbey founded 1115 under Bernard, from which sixty-eight daughter houses were planted)
etymology: French clair val, the bright valley, Latinised Clara Vallis; the valley was called Wormwood before the monks renamed it.
biblical_def: Clairvaux was founded in 1115 as the third daughter of Citeaux, and its first abbot was Bernard, twenty-five years old at his appointment and the dominant churchman in Europe for the next forty years. Sixty-eight houses were founded directly from Clairvaux in his lifetime, and over three hundred traced descent from it. Bernard preached the Second Crusade, pursued Abelard, intervened in a papal schism, and wrote the sermons on the Song of Songs and the treatises on grace and free will and on loving God. The dictionary records Clairvaux chiefly for Bernard's theology, because he is the medieval writer the Reformers treated with most respect. Calvin quotes him approvingly on justification and Luther called him the best of the fathers since the apostles, and the reason is plain in Bernard's own words on where a man's confidence rests — not in his merits but in God's mercy. “not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law” (Phi 3:9) is Paul's version of Bernard's best instinct, and “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8) with “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9) is the doctrine he came nearest to stating outright.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines merit as desert of reward; mercy as compassion shown to an offender; a crusade as a holy war; grace as the free favour of God; and free will as the power of choosing.
webster_full: MERIT, n. Desert; goodness or excellence which entitles one to honor or reward.
MERCY, n. That benevolence, mildness or tenderness of heart which disposes a person to overlook injuries, or to treat an offender better than he deserves.
CRUSADE, n. A military expedition undertaken by Christians for the recovery of the Holy Land from the infidels.
GRACE, n. The free unmerited love and favour of God, the spring and source of all the benefits men receive from him.
FREE-WILL, n. The power of directing our own actions without constraint by necessity or fate.
scriptures: Phi 3:9
And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith:
Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Eph 2:9
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
Rom 3:28
Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.
corruption_summary: Cistercian abbey of 1115 whose first abbot Bernard planted sixty-eight houses and whose theology the Reformers cited with respect.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Bernard belongs in a Reformed reading list. His settled position was that a man's confidence rests on mercy and not on desert, which is Paul's own renunciation, “not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law” (Phi 3:9), and very nearly the apostolic formula itself, “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8).

The live temptation is to adopt Bernard whole, crusade preaching and Marian devotion included, or to discard him whole because of them. The dictionary does neither. Where he says “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9) in his own idiom he is to be followed, and where he adds a mediatrix beside Christ he is to be refused, because “a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28) admits no supplement.

pos: n. (the Norman abbey refounded 1001, holder of a relic of the Precious Blood)
etymology: From a Germanic or Gaulish form, probably fisc and camp, the fish field; Latinised Fiscannum.
biblical_def: Fecamp on the Normandy coast had a nunnery from the seventh century, destroyed by Vikings, and was refounded as a Benedictine abbey in 1001 by Duke Richard II, who brought in William of Volpiano, the reformer from Dijon, to govern it. Under him and his successors Fecamp became the leading monastery of Normandy, the burial place of the early dukes, and a centre of learning. Its chief draw was a relic: a phial said to contain the Precious Blood of Christ, carried, legend said, from Jerusalem and washed ashore in a fig trunk. Pilgrims came in numbers, and the Trinity of Fecamp was celebrated with its own feast. The dictionary records Fecamp beside Hailes, since the two relics make the same claim and invite the same answer. Hailes' phial was examined in 1539 and pronounced a confection; Fecamp's was never tested. But the objection does not depend on chemistry. The blood of Christ is applied by faith and not by proximity, and “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8) with “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9) leaves a phial no office to perform.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a relic as the remains of a saint preserved with superstitious reverence; a phial as a small glass vessel; a legend as a chronicle of a saint's life; veneration as the highest degree of respect; and application as the act of applying.
webster_full: RELIC, n. The remains of the body of a saint, or some part of his garments, preserved with a superstitious reverence.
PHIAL, n. A glass vessel or bottle; a small glass vessel used particularly for medicines.
LEGEND, n. A chronicle or register of the lives of saints, formerly read at matins.
VENERATION, n. The highest degree of respect and reverence; respect mingled with some degree of awe.
APPLICATION, n. The act of applying or laying on; the thing applied.
scriptures: Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Eph 2:9
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
Gal 2:16

Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified.
Joh 4:24
God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.
corruption_summary: Leading Norman Benedictine abbey refounded in 1001, holder of a relic of the Precious Blood and a major pilgrimage destination.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is how the blood of Christ reaches a sinner. It is not by being near it. The apostolic account is “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8), guarded at once by “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9), which leaves no function for a phial however authentic.

The live temptation is to argue about the relic's provenance as though that were the question. Fecamp's was never tested and Hailes' failed, and it makes no difference to the doctrine: “a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ” (Gal 2:16). Christ also declines to attach worship to any location, “God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.” (Joh 4:24), which disposes of the pilgrimage as such.

pos: n. (the Burgundian abbey whose claim to the relics of Mary Magdalene made it a pilgrimage capital, and collapsed in 1279)
etymology: From the Latin estate name Vercellacus or Vizeliacum; the hill town takes the abbey's name.
biblical_def: Vezelay in Burgundy claimed from the eleventh century to hold the body of Mary Magdalene, brought it was said from Provence, and the claim made it one of the four great assembly points for pilgrims bound for Compostela and one of the richest churches in France. The abbey built the Madeleine, with its carved narthex tympanum of Pentecost; Bernard preached the Second Crusade there in 1146, and Richard the Lionheart and Philip Augustus mustered there for the Third. Then in 1279 a rival claim at Saint-Maximin in Provence was endorsed by Charles of Anjou and accepted at Rome, and Vezelay's pilgrimage collapsed within a generation. The dictionary records Vezelay for that collapse, because it is the relic economy auditing itself. Two churches claimed one body, one was preferred for political reasons, and the losing town emptied. Nothing in the episode turned on evidence. “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21) is the duty that was never discharged, and “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men” (Col 2:8) names what had been built in its place.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a narthex is not in Webster, but a portico is defined as a covered walk; a tympanum as the panel of a pediment; translation as the removal of a saint's relics; a rival as one who competes; and imposture as deception under a false character.
webster_full: PORTICO, n. In architecture, a kind of gallery on the ground, or a piazza encompassed with arches supported by columns.
TYMPANUM, n. The drum of the ear; in architecture, the area of a pediment.
TRANSLATION, n. The removal of the body or relics of a saint to another place.
RIVAL, n. One who is in pursuit of the same object as another; a competitor.
IMPOSTURE, n. Deception practiced under a false or assumed character; fraud or imposition.
scriptures: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
Joh 4:24
God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.
Eph 2:9
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
corruption_summary: Burgundian abbey whose claim to Mary Magdalene's relics made it a pilgrimage capital until a rival Provencal claim was endorsed in 1279.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the relic trade was never settled by evidence. Two churches held one body and a prince decided between them. The duty Paul lays on a congregation is the one nobody performed: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21).

The live temptation is to treat Vezelay's fall as a one-off embarrassment rather than a verdict on the system. Paul's warning is general and structural, “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men” (Col 2:8). And the whole apparatus is beside the point from the start, since worship is fixed by “God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.” (Joh 4:24) and standing before God by “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9).

pos: n. (the French cathedral city whose twelfth-century school taught a generation, and whose glass survives nearly entire)
etymology: From the Gaulish tribe the Carnutes, through Latin Carnotum; the French form drops the final consonants in speech.
biblical_def: Chartres, south-west of Paris, was from the early eleventh century one of the leading cathedral schools of Europe. Bernard of Chartres, Thierry of Chartres and William of Conches taught there, and John of Salisbury, afterwards bishop of Chartres, left in his Metalogicon the best surviving account of how such a school worked — the grammar, the set authors, the slow reading. The cathedral itself burned in 1194, all but the west front and the crypt, which held the Sancta Camisa, a garment venerated as the Virgin's; the rebuilding was financed partly by pilgrims to that relic and completed with extraordinary speed, and it retains more of its original thirteenth-century glass than any other great church in France. The dictionary records Chartres for the school and the glass. The school was a genuine good, and the dictionary says so: “Study to shew thyself approved unto God” (2Ti 2:15) is a command, and “whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just” (Phi 4:8) licenses the attention these men gave to grammar and the poets. The relic that paid for the windows is another matter, and “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9) settles it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a school as a place of instruction; grammar as the art of speaking correctly; glass as a hard brittle transparent substance; a cloister school is given under school; and a garment as an article of clothing.
webster_full: SCHOOL, n. A place or house in which persons are instructed in arts, science, languages or any species of learning.
GRAMMAR, n. The art of speaking or writing a language with propriety or correctness, according to established usage.
GLASS, n. A hard, brittle, transparent, factitious substance, formed by fusing sand with fixed alkalies.
DIALECTIC, a. Logical; argumental; pertaining to the art of reasoning.
GARMENT, n. Any article of clothing, as a coat, a gown, &c.
scriptures: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
Phi 4:8

Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
Eph 2:9
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
corruption_summary: French cathedral city with a leading twelfth-century school and the most complete surviving medieval glass in France, rebuilt after the fire of 1194.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that careful learning is commanded, not merely tolerated. Paul tells Timothy to “Study to shew thyself approved unto God” (2Ti 2:15), and Philippians licenses the whole range of honest attention, “whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just” (Phi 4:8). The school of Chartres, teaching boys to read Virgil slowly, was doing something a Reformed conscience can approve.

The live temptation is to let the beauty of the result cover the means. The windows were paid for in part by pilgrims coming to a venerated garment, and that transaction is excluded by “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9). Chartres is therefore two things at once, and the rule for sorting them is “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16) — the measure the school itself professed to serve.
